He visits me, and takes the snow, and moulds
Women and men, like thee; and breathes into them

Alone and sad.

321. fire and snow] Baker, ‘Spenser and The Witch of Atlas’ 477 cps Spenser, Colin Clovts come home
againe ll. 835–50. The Witch’s geographical location may also be at issue: To the Nile (Longman ii
349–50, no. 163) ll. 3–5 refers to the extremes of cold and heat associated with Atlas’s geographical
location and height.
 322. repugnant] This usage draws attention to the word’s Latin root in pugnare (to fight). The antago-
nism of fire and snow towards one another is to be overcome by a third element, ‘love’, in l. 323. This
idea, and the generally medicinal qualities associated with the Witch’s presence, parallel the definition
of love in Eryximachus’ speech in Symposium 186c — 186e: ‘The science of medicine, in a word, is a
knowledge of the love affairs of the body . . . the most skilful physician . . . ought to make those things
which are most inimical, friendly, and excite them to mutual love . . . . Our progenitor, Aesculapius . . .
